name: DORA — Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience

sources.scope: Entity-facing obligations only. The oversight framework for critical ICT third-party providers (Articles 31–44) creates duties for the European Supervisory Authorities rather than for financial entities, and is not assessed here. The simplified framework at Article 16 is not modelled — entities in scope of it should exclude the items that do not apply and note the exclusion.
sources.crosswalk: Indicative mapping to NIST CSF 2.0, maintained in this file

levels.d: No evidence the outcome is addressed.
Documented, approved and applied across scope.
Measured, reviewed and enforced with evidence.
Continuously improved against metrics and threat change.

effort.M: Medium — project effort using existing tooling
effort.H: High — new capability, tooling or budget required

priority.d: More than 2.0 below the target maturity
At or above target — sustain the control

groups.name: Chapter II — ICT risk management
groups.desc: Governance, the ICT risk management framework, and the identify, protect, detect, respond and learn requirements of Articles 5 to 14.

sections.name: Governance and framework (Art. 5–7)
sections.desc: Management body accountability, the ICT risk management framework, resilience strategy and system adequacy.

controls.text: Art. 6.4 Internal audit of the framework
Art. 7 ICT systems, protocols and tools

sections.name: Identification (Art. 8)
sections.desc: Functions, assets, risk sources, critical function mapping and the third-party dependency register.

controls.text: Art. 8.1 Identification of functions and assets
Art. 8.6 Register of ICT third-party dependencies

sections.name: Protection and prevention (Art. 9)
sections.desc: Monitoring and control, resilience by design, and the required security policies.

controls.text: Art. 9.4a Data and system security policies

sections.name: Detection (Art. 10)
sections.desc: Anomaly detection, alert thresholds and detection resourcing.

sections.name: Response, recovery and backup (Art. 11–12)
sections.desc: ICT business continuity, response and recovery plans, testing, crisis management and backup arrangements.

sections.name: Learning and communication (Art. 13–14)
sections.desc: Threat and vulnerability intelligence, post-incident review, continuous improvement, training and communication plans.

controls.text: Art. 13.1 Information gathering on vulnerabilities and threats

groups.name: Chapter III — ICT incident management
groups.desc: Incident management process, classification against the DORA criteria, and the reporting obligations of Articles 17 to 23.

sections.name: Incident management process (Art. 17)
sections.desc: Process definition, recording, early warning, triage, roles, communication, escalation and root cause.

sections.name: Classification (Art. 18)
sections.desc: Classification of incidents and significant cyber threats against the regulatory criteria.

sections.name: Reporting (Art. 19, 23)
sections.desc: Reporting major incidents to the competent authority, the reporting timeline, client notification and payment-related incidents.

controls.text: Art. 19.3 Initial, intermediate and final reports

groups.name: Chapter IV — Digital operational resilience testing
groups.desc: The testing programme, the range of tests required, and threat-led penetration testing under Articles 24 to 27.

sections.name: Testing programme (Art. 24–25)
sections.desc: Programme establishment, risk-based scoping, independence, annual coverage, remediation and the range of test types.

controls.text: Art. 24.5 Annual testing of critical systems

sections.name: Threat-led penetration testing (Art. 26–27)
sections.desc: TLPT frequency and scope, inclusion of third parties, and tester requirements.

groups.name: Chapter V — ICT third-party risk
groups.desc: Third-party risk principles, the register of information, pre-contractual assessment, concentration risk and contractual provisions under Articles 28 to 30.

sections.name: Principles and register (Art. 28)
sections.desc: Full responsibility, strategy and policy, register of information, pre-contract assessment, termination rights and exit strategies.

sections.name: Concentration and contracts (Art. 29–30)
sections.desc: Concentration risk assessment and the key contractual provisions, including enhanced terms for critical functions.

groups.name: Chapter VI — Information sharing
groups.desc: Voluntary cyber threat information-sharing arrangements under Article 45.

references.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
references.note: Indicative crosswalk to NIST CSF 2.0, so DORA findings can also be reported against a technical control framework. It is not an official mapping. DORA obligations that are purely regulatory — reporting deadlines, register submission, contractual terms — have no meaningful CSF counterpart and are left unmapped.

items.q: Does the management body define, approve, oversee and remain accountable for the implementation of all ICT risk management framework arrangements?
items.rec: Record management body approval of the ICT risk management framework and evidence ongoing oversight through minuted review, not one-off sign-off. Accountability under DORA sits with the management body personally and cannot be delegated to IT.

items.q: Does the management body set roles for ICT functions, approve and review the digital operational resilience strategy, approve ICT third-party arrangements, and allocate budget to ICT resilience?
items.rec: Map each management body duty listed in Article 5(2) to a named forum and evidence trail — role approval, business continuity and audit policy approval, third-party arrangements, budget allocation and incident reporting lines.

items.q: Do management body members actively keep up to date with sufficient knowledge and skills to understand and assess ICT risk and its impact?
items.rec: Provide and record regular ICT risk training for management body members, with content specific to the entity's own ICT risk profile rather than generic awareness.

items.q: Is a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework in place as part of the overall risk management system?
items.rec: Document a single ICT risk management framework covering strategies, policies, procedures, protocols and tools, positioned explicitly within the overall risk management system.

items.q: Is the ICT risk management framework reviewed at least annually, and upon major incidents, supervisory instruction or conclusions from resilience testing?
items.rec: Schedule the annual framework review and define the trigger events — major ICT incidents, supervisory instructions, testing or audit conclusions — that force an out-of-cycle review.

items.q: Is the ICT risk management framework subject to internal audit by auditors with sufficient ICT knowledge, on a risk-based audit plan?
items.rec: Include the ICT risk management framework in the internal audit plan, resourced with demonstrable ICT competence, and operate a formal follow-up process for audit findings.

items.q: Is a digital operational resilience strategy documented, setting out how the framework is implemented, including risk tolerance for ICT disruption?
items.rec: Produce a digital operational resilience strategy stating ICT risk tolerance, information security objectives, reference architecture, detection mechanisms, resilience testing plans and third-party strategy.

items.q: Where relevant, is a multi-vendor strategy documented showing key dependencies and the rationale for the mix of providers?
items.rec: Document the multi-vendor strategy including key dependencies on ICT third-party providers and the rationale for the provider mix, or record why a single-vendor approach is acceptable.

items.q: Are ICT systems, protocols and tools appropriate, reliable, of sufficient capacity, and technologically resilient to handle peak processing and stress conditions?
items.rec: Evidence that ICT systems are kept up to date, have sufficient capacity for peak and stressed conditions, and are technologically resilient — capacity testing results are the practical evidence here.

items.q: Are all ICT-supported business functions, roles and responsibilities, information assets and ICT assets identified, classified and documented?
items.rec: Maintain a classified inventory of business functions, information assets and ICT assets, with configurations and interconnections documented and reviewed at least annually.

items.q: Are all sources of ICT risk identified and assessed, in particular exposure to and from other entities, at least annually?
items.rec: Assess sources of ICT risk at least annually, explicitly including risk exposure to and from other financial entities, and record the assessment.

items.q: Are all information and ICT assets supporting critical or important functions identified, together with their interdependencies?
items.rec: Identify critical or important functions and map the assets, processes and third parties they depend on, so that resilience effort is directed by criticality.

items.q: Are risk assessments performed and documented upon each major change in network and information system infrastructure or processes?
items.rec: Make an ICT risk assessment a mandatory, evidenced gate for major infrastructure and process changes, not only for projects.

items.q: Is a register maintained of all processes dependent on ICT third-party service providers, including identified interconnections?
items.rec: Maintain the register of information on ICT third-party arrangements in the format required by the supervisor, covering all providers and identifying those supporting critical or important functions.

items.q: Are ICT systems continuously monitored and controlled to minimise the impact of ICT risk, including through appropriate security tools and policies?
items.rec: Deploy continuous monitoring across ICT systems with defined ownership for alert review, and document the security tools, policies and procedures relied upon.

items.q: Are ICT security strategies, policies, procedures, protocols and tools designed to ensure resilience, continuity and availability, and to maintain high standards of data availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality?
items.rec: Document how design decisions deliver availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality, including data at rest, in use and in transit.

items.q: Are policies in place ensuring the security of the means of transfer of data and limiting the risk of corruption, loss, unauthorised access and technical flaws?
items.rec: Maintain policies covering secure data transfer, protection against corruption and loss, and prevention of unauthorised access and technical flaws hindering business activity.

items.q: Are policies implemented that limit physical and virtual access to ICT resources to what is required for legitimate and approved functions, based on need-to-know and least privilege?
items.rec: Implement access management on need-to-know, need-to-use and least-privilege principles, covering physical and logical access with periodic recertification.

items.q: Are strong authentication mechanisms implemented, based on relevant standards and dedicated control systems, together with protective measures for cryptographic keys?
items.rec: Enforce strong authentication aligned to recognised standards for all remote, privileged and critical system access, and document the cryptographic key protection measures.

items.q: Are documented change management procedures in place for changes to software, hardware, firmware, systems and security parameters, based on a risk assessment approach?
items.rec: Operate documented ICT change management covering software, hardware, firmware and security parameters, with risk assessment, approval, verification and rollback for all environments.

items.q: Are appropriate and comprehensive policies for patches and updates documented and applied?
items.rec: Maintain a documented patch and update policy with SLAs by severity, covering operating systems, applications, firmware and network devices, and report compliance against SLA.

items.q: Are mechanisms in place to promptly detect anomalous activities, including ICT network performance issues and ICT-related incidents, and to identify potential material single points of failure?
items.rec: Deploy detection covering anomalous activity, network performance degradation and single points of failure, with correlation across sources rather than isolated tool consoles.

items.q: Do detection mechanisms enable multiple layers of control, define alert thresholds and criteria to trigger incident response processes, and include automatic alert mechanisms?
items.rec: Define and document alert thresholds and the criteria that trigger the incident response process, tuning them away from vendor defaults on a review cycle.

items.q: Are sufficient resources and capabilities devoted to monitoring user activity, occurrence of ICT anomalies and ICT-related incidents, in particular cyber-attacks?
items.rec: Establish resourced monitoring of user activity and ICT anomalies with defined coverage hours, using a managed detection service where in-house out-of-hours cover is not viable.

items.q: Is a dedicated and comprehensive ICT business continuity policy in place as an integral part of the operational business continuity policy?
items.rec: Document a dedicated ICT business continuity policy, approved by the management body and integrated with the wider operational continuity policy.

items.q: Are ICT business continuity plans implemented to ensure continuity of critical or important functions, respond to and resolve incidents, and estimate impacts, losses and damages?
items.rec: Maintain ICT continuity plans that quantify preliminary impacts, losses and damages, and define activation criteria for critical or important functions.

items.q: Are ICT response and recovery plans established, documented, and subject to independent internal audit review?
items.rec: Document ICT response and recovery plans covering all critical or important functions, and include them in the internal audit scope.

items.q: Are ICT business continuity and response and recovery plans tested at least annually, including switchover scenarios between primary and secondary infrastructure?
items.rec: Test continuity and recovery plans at least annually with realistic scenarios, including switchover between primary and redundant infrastructure, and evidence the results.

items.q: Is a crisis management function established that sets out clear procedures to manage internal and external crisis communications?
items.rec: Establish a named crisis management function with documented internal and external communication procedures and decision authority.

items.q: Are readily accessible records of activities before and during disruption events kept when continuity plans are activated?
items.rec: Maintain a contemporaneous, timestamped record of activities before and during disruption, held where it will remain accessible when primary systems are down.

items.q: Are backup policies and procedures, and restoration and recovery procedures and methods, developed and documented, specifying scope and minimum frequency based on criticality?
items.rec: Document backup scope and frequency driven by information criticality, alongside restoration and recovery methods with defined recovery point and time objectives.

items.q: Are backup systems physically and logically segregated from source systems and not directly accessible from them?
items.rec: Segregate backup systems physically and logically from source systems, using immutable or offline copies not reachable with production credentials.

items.q: Where recovery uses secondary systems, are they maintained at an adequate distance and with sufficient resources and security to ensure continuity of critical functions?
items.rec: Confirm secondary site geographic separation, capability and security are adequate for the risk profile and can sustain critical functions, not merely hold data.

items.q: Are backup and restoration and recovery procedures periodically tested, including restoration from backups using isolated ICT systems?
items.rec: Test restoration periodically using isolated systems rather than production, and include at least one full system recovery each year.

items.q: Are capabilities and staff in place to gather information on vulnerabilities, cyber threats, and ICT-related incidents, and to analyse their likely impacts?
items.rec: Formalise vulnerability and threat information gathering with named ownership, and document how the analysis of likely impact feeds the risk framework.

items.q: Are post ICT-related incident reviews conducted after major incidents, analysing the causes of disruption and identifying required improvements?
items.rec: Require post-incident review after every major incident, examining the promptness of response, quality of forensics and effectiveness of escalation, with actions tracked.

items.q: Are the findings from post-incident reviews and testing incorporated into the ICT risk assessment process, and reported to the management body?
items.rec: Feed post-incident review and testing findings back into the risk assessment process, and report the resulting changes to the management body.

items.q: Are ICT security awareness programmes and digital operational resilience training mandatory modules in staff training schemes, including for the management body?
items.rec: Make ICT security awareness and digital operational resilience training mandatory for all staff and the management body, with completion tracked and content matched to role.

items.q: Are communication plans in place enabling responsible disclosure of major incidents or vulnerabilities to clients, counterparts and the public, with at least one person tasked with implementing the communication strategy?
items.rec: Document communication plans for clients, counterparties and the public, and name the person responsible for the communication strategy and acting as public spokesperson.

items.q: Is an ICT-related incident management process defined, established and implemented to detect, manage and notify ICT-related incidents?
items.rec: Establish a documented ICT-related incident management process covering detection, management and notification, aligned to the DORA classification criteria.

items.q: Are all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats recorded, with relevant incidents monitored to ensure causes are identified, documented and addressed?
items.rec: Record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats in a single register, and track root cause identification and remediation to closure.

items.q: Do incident management procedures establish early warning indicators?
items.rec: Define early warning indicators that precede material ICT disruption, and monitor them proactively rather than relying on failure alerts.

items.q: Are procedures established to identify, track, log, categorise and classify ICT-related incidents according to priority, severity and criticality of affected services?
items.rec: Document triage criteria and mandate severity and criticality classification on every incident record, auditing compliance periodically.

items.q: Are roles and responsibilities assigned for different ICT-related incident types and scenarios?
items.rec: Assign incident roles by scenario type with named deputies, and rehearse them so assignment translates into capability.

items.q: Are plans set out for communication to staff, external stakeholders, media and, where relevant, clients, counterparts and the public?
items.rec: Prepare and rehearse incident communication plans for each stakeholder group, with pre-approved holding statements.

items.q: Are major ICT-related incidents reported to relevant senior management, with the management body informed of impact, response and additional controls?
items.rec: Define reporting thresholds and timeframes for informing senior management and the management body of major incidents, and evidence they were met.

items.q: Are procedures established to identify, document and address the root cause of incidents and prevent recurrence?
items.rec: Mandate root cause analysis for incidents above the defined threshold, with preventive actions tracked in the improvement register.

items.q: Are ICT-related incidents classified against the DORA criteria — clients affected, duration and service downtime, geographical spread, data losses, criticality of services affected, and economic impact?
items.rec: Embed the six DORA classification criteria directly into the incident record so that major-incident determination is a documented calculation rather than a judgement call.

items.q: Are cyber threats classified as significant based on the criticality of services at risk, the number or relevance of entities or clients targeted, and their potential impact?
items.rec: Define and apply criteria for classifying a cyber threat as significant, and document the decision when the voluntary notification route is considered.

items.q: Are major ICT-related incidents reported to the relevant competent authority?
items.rec: Confirm the competent authority, the reporting channel and the authorised submitter, and rehearse submission so the route is proven before it is needed.

items.q: Are initial notification, intermediate report and final report submitted within the applicable deadlines?
items.rec: Build the initial, intermediate and final reporting deadlines into the incident process with automated reminders, and hold report templates ready to complete.

items.q: Where a major ICT-related incident has an impact on the financial interests of clients, are clients informed without undue delay, along with measures taken to mitigate adverse effects?
items.rec: Define the trigger and route for client notification where financial interests are affected, and pre-approve the notification content.

items.q: Are operational or security payment-related incidents managed and reported under the same incident management process?
items.rec: Confirm payment-related operational and security incidents are captured by the same process and meet the applicable reporting obligations.

items.q: Is a sound and comprehensive digital operational resilience testing programme established as an integral part of the ICT risk management framework?
items.rec: Establish a documented resilience testing programme covering assessments, tests, methodologies, practices and tools, rather than commissioning isolated tests.

items.q: Does the testing programme follow a risk-based approach, taking into account the evolving ICT risk landscape and the criticality of information assets and services?
items.rec: Drive test scope and frequency from asset criticality and the current threat landscape, and document the rationale each cycle.

items.q: Is testing undertaken by independent parties, whether internal or external, with conflicts of interest managed throughout the design and execution of tests?
items.rec: Use independent testers and document how conflicts of interest are avoided where internal resources conduct testing.

items.q: Are appropriate tests conducted on all ICT systems and applications supporting critical or important functions at least annually?
items.rec: Ensure every ICT system supporting a critical or important function is tested at least annually, tracked against the asset inventory to prove coverage.

items.q: Are procedures and policies in place to prioritise, classify and remediate all issues revealed throughout the performance of tests, with internal validation methodologies?
items.rec: Track test findings in the central remediation register with prioritisation, SLA and documented internal validation that fixes are effective.

items.q: Does testing include, as appropriate, vulnerability assessments and scans, open source analyses, network security assessments, gap analyses, physical security reviews, source code reviews, scenario-based tests, compatibility, performance and end-to-end testing, and penetration testing?
items.rec: Map the DORA testing catalogue against what is actually performed, and document a justification where a test type is not applicable.

items.q: Where required, is advanced threat-led penetration testing carried out at least every three years, covering several or all critical or important functions on live production systems?
items.rec: Confirm whether TLPT applies to the entity and, if so, plan the three-yearly cycle covering critical or important functions on live production systems.

items.q: Are ICT third-party service providers supporting critical or important functions included in the scope of threat-led penetration testing?
items.rec: Secure contractual rights to include critical ICT third parties in TLPT scope, or obtain pooled testing evidence where the provider offers it.

items.q: Do testers meet the required standards of suitability, reputation, technical and organisational capability, independence and certification?
items.rec: Document tester selection criteria covering suitability, reputation, capability, independence and relevant accreditation, and retain the evidence per engagement.

items.q: Is ICT third-party risk managed as an integral component of ICT risk, in accordance with the principle of full responsibility for compliance regardless of outsourcing?
items.rec: State explicitly in policy that outsourcing does not transfer regulatory responsibility, and manage third-party ICT risk inside the ICT risk framework rather than alongside it.

items.q: Is a strategy on ICT third-party risk adopted and reviewed regularly, including a policy on the use of ICT services supporting critical or important functions?
items.rec: Adopt a management-body-approved ICT third-party risk strategy and a specific policy for services supporting critical or important functions, reviewed at least annually.

items.q: Is a register of information maintained on all contractual arrangements for ICT services, distinguishing those supporting critical or important functions, and reported to the competent authority annually?
items.rec: Maintain the register of information in the supervisory template, updated on contract change, and submit it annually along with notification of new arrangements for critical functions.

items.q: Before entering an arrangement, is an assessment performed of criticality, supervisory conditions, concentration risk, due diligence on the provider, and conflicts of interest?
items.rec: Introduce a mandatory pre-contract assessment gate covering criticality, concentration risk, provider due diligence and conflicts of interest, with the outcome recorded.

items.q: Are contractual arrangements able to be terminated on defined grounds, including material breach, circumstances impeding performance, provider weaknesses, and supervisory instruction?
items.rec: Ensure ICT contracts contain the DORA termination rights, and record any contract that does not so the gap is visible at renewal.

items.q: Are exit strategies in place for ICT services supporting critical or important functions, including transition plans and sufficiently tested alternatives?
items.rec: Document a tested exit strategy per critical ICT service, covering transition plan, alternative provider or in-house capability, and data return.

items.q: Is ICT concentration risk assessed, including reliance on providers that are not easily substitutable, and the risk arising from multiple arrangements with the same provider?
items.rec: Assess and record ICT concentration risk including substitutability and sub-outsourcing chains, and set a documented tolerance for it.

items.q: Do contracts include the required elements — service description, data processing locations, data protection provisions, access and audit rights, service levels, assistance during incidents, and termination and exit provisions?
items.rec: Produce a DORA-compliant contractual schedule covering the Article 30(2) elements and apply it to all new and renewing ICT contracts.

items.q: For services supporting critical or important functions, do contracts additionally include full service level descriptions, notice periods, reporting obligations, incident assistance, participation in TLPT and unrestricted audit rights?
items.rec: Apply the enhanced Article 30(3) terms to every contract supporting a critical or important function, and record any gap as a tracked risk pending renewal.

items.q: Where the entity participates in cyber threat information-sharing arrangements, are they operated within trusted communities with appropriate protection for the information shared?
items.rec: Where participating in information-sharing arrangements, document the community, the protections applied to shared information, and notify the competent authority of membership.
